summary.text: Legendre’s formula reduces divisibility to the floor inequality \(\lfloor K/q\rfloor+\lfloor L/q\rfloor+2\lfloor(K+L)/q\rfloor\le \lfloor3K/q\rfloor+\lfloor3L/q\rfloor\), proved by decomposing \(K,L\) into quotients and remainders; this handles every prime after taking \(K=4n+2\) and \(L=2n+3\). The extra factor \(108=2^2 3^3\) is obtained by sharpening the \(2\)-adic inequalities at powers \(2\) and \(4\), and by using \(v_3((3a+2)!)=v_3(a!)+a\) together with \(v_3(a!)\le a/2\) for the \(3\)-adic bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
K=4n+2,\qquad L=2n+3,\qquad M=K+L=6n+5.
\]
Then
\[
3K=12n+6,\qquad 3L=6n+9.
\]
Thus the desired assertion is
\[
108\,K!L!(M!)^2\mid (3K)!(3L)!.
\]
We prove this prime by prime.

For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(x\). We repeatedly use Legendre’s formula
\[
v_p(t!)=\sum_{i\ge 1}\left\lfloor\frac{t}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Only finitely many terms in this sum are nonzero. We also use the standard divisibility criterion: for positive integers \(A,B\), one has \(A\mid B\) if and only if \(v_p(A)\le v_p(B)\) for every prime \(p\).

We first establish a general floor inequality which explains the basic factorial ratio.

### 1. A general floor inequality

For every positive integer \(q\) and all nonnegative integers \(K,L\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac Kq\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac Lq\right\rfloor+
2\left\lfloor\frac{K+L}{q}\right\rfloor
\le
\left\lfloor\frac{3K}{q}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{3L}{q}\right\rfloor.
\tag{1}
\]

To prove this, write
\[
K=aq+r,\qquad L=bq+s,
\]
where \(0\le r,s<q\). Then
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{3K}{q}\right\rfloor
=3a+\left\lfloor\frac{3r}{q}\right\rfloor,
\]
with the analogous formula for \(L\), while
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{K+L}{q}\right\rfloor
=a+b+\left\lfloor\frac{r+s}{q}\right\rfloor.
\]
After cancelling the common contribution \(3a+3b\), inequality (1) reduces to
\[
2\left\lfloor\frac{r+s}{q}\right\rfloor
\le
\left\lfloor\frac{3r}{q}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{3s}{q}\right\rfloor.
\tag{2}
\]

If \(r+s<q\), the left side of (2) is zero, so the result is immediate. Suppose instead that \(r+s\ge q\). Since \(r,s<q\), we have \(r+s<2q\), and hence the left side of (2) is exactly \(2\). If both \(3r\ge q\) and \(3s\ge q\), each floor on the right is at least \(1\), so their sum is at least \(2\). If, say, \(3s<q\), then from \(3r+3s\ge 3q\) we obtain \(3r>2q\), so \(\lfloor 3r/q\rfloor\ge2\). The case \(3r<q\) is symmetric. Thus (2), and consequently (1), always holds.

Taking \(q=p^i\) in (1), summing over \(i\ge1\), and applying Legendre’s formula gives, for every prime \(p\),
\[
v_p(K!)+v_p(L!)+2v_p((K+L)!)
\le v_p((3K)!)+v_p((3L)!).
\tag{3}
\]
Therefore, for arbitrary nonnegative \(K,L\),
\[
K!L!((K+L)!)^2\mid (3K)!(3L)!.
\tag{4}
\]
For our particular \(K=4n+2\) and \(L=2n+3\), this already proves the required valuation inequality at every prime not dividing \(108\). Since
\[
108=2^2 3^3,
\]
it remains to obtain two additional factors of \(2\) and three additional factors of \(3\).

### 2. The two additional factors of \(2\)

We prove
\[
2+v_2(K!)+v_2(L!)+2v_2(M!)
\le v_2((3K)!)+v_2((3L)!).
\tag{5}
\]
By Legendre’s formula, it is enough to strengthen the summand inequality (1) by one unit at \(q=2\), strengthen it by one more unit at \(q=4\), and use (1) unchanged for all other powers of \(2\).

For \(q=2\), the relevant floors can be evaluated directly:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left\lfloor\frac K2\right\rfloor&=2n+1,&
\left\lfloor\frac L2\right\rfloor&=n+1,&
\left\lfloor\frac M2\right\rfloor&=3n+2,\\
\left\lfloor\frac{3K}{2}\right\rfloor&=6n+3,&
\left\lfloor\frac{3L}{2}\right\rfloor&=3n+4.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
1+
\left\lfloor\frac K2\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac L2\right\rfloor+
2\left\lfloor\frac M2\right\rfloor
=9n+7
=
\left\lfloor\frac{3K}{2}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{3L}{2}\right\rfloor.
\tag{6}
\]
Thus the \(i=1\) summand has one unit of extra room.

For \(q=4\), we split according to the parity of \(n\).

If \(n=2m\), then
\[
K=8m+2,\qquad L=4m+3,\qquad M=12m+5,
\]
and hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left\lfloor\frac K4\right\rfloor&=2m,&
\left\lfloor\frac L4\right\rfloor&=m,&
\left\lfloor\frac M4\right\rfloor&=3m+1,\\
\left\lfloor\frac{3K}{4}\right\rfloor&=6m+1,&
\left\lfloor\frac{3L}{4}\right\rfloor&=3m+2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
1+
\left\lfloor\frac K4\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac L4\right\rfloor+
2\left\lfloor\frac M4\right\rfloor
=9m+3
=
\left\lfloor\frac{3K}{4}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{3L}{4}\right\rfloor.
\tag{7}
\]

If \(n=2m+1\), then
\[
K=8m+6,\qquad L=4m+5,\qquad M=12m+11,
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left\lfloor\frac K4\right\rfloor&=2m+1,&
\left\lfloor\frac L4\right\rfloor&=m+1,&
\left\lfloor\frac M4\right\rfloor&=3m+2,\\
\left\lfloor\frac{3K}{4}\right\rfloor&=6m+4,&
\left\lfloor\frac{3L}{4}\right\rfloor&=3m+3.
\end{aligned}
\]
It follows that
\[
1+
\left\lfloor\frac K4\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac L4\right\rfloor+
2\left\lfloor\frac M4\right\rfloor
=9m+7
=
\left\lfloor\frac{3K}{4}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{3L}{4}\right\rfloor.
\tag{8}
\]
Thus the \(i=2\) summand also has one unit of extra room, regardless of the parity of \(n\).

For every \(i\ge1\) with \(i\ne1,2\), apply (1) with \(q=2^i\). Summing those inequalities together with (6) and either (7) or (8) gives exactly (5). Since \(v_2(108)=2\), this proves
\[
v_2\bigl(108K!L!(M!)^2\bigr)
\le v_2\bigl((3K)!(3L)!\bigr).
\tag{9}
\]

### 3. The three additional factors of \(3\)

We next prove
\[
3+v_3(K!)+v_3(L!)+2v_3(M!)
\le v_3((3K)!)+v_3((3L)!).
\tag{10}
\]

For every nonnegative integer \(t\), Legendre’s formula gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_3((3t)!)
&=\left\lfloor\frac{3t}{3}\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\frac{3t}{3^2}\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\frac{3t}{3^3}\right\rfloor+\cdots\\
&=t+\left\lfloor\frac t3\right\rfloor
 +\left\lfloor\frac t{3^2}\right\rfloor+\cdots\\
&=t+v_3(t!).
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]
Applying this with \(t=K\) and \(t=L\), the right side of (10) becomes
\[
v_3(K!)+K+v_3(L!)+L
=v_3(K!)+v_3(L!)+M.
\]
Thus, after cancelling \(v_3(K!)+v_3(L!)\), inequality (10) is equivalent to
\[
3+2v_3(M!)\le M.
\tag{12}
\]

We now prove (12). Put
\[
a=2n+1.
\]
Then \(a\) is odd and
\[
M=6n+5=3a+2.
\]
Neither \(3a+1\) nor \(3a+2\) is divisible by \(3\), so adjoining these last two factors to \((3a)!\) does not change the 3-adic valuation. Hence, using (11),
\[
v_3(M!)=v_3((3a+2)!)=v_3((3a)!)=a+v_3(a!).
\tag{13}
\]

Legendre’s formula also yields the elementary bound
\[
v_3(a!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{a}{3^i}\right\rfloor
\le \sum_{i\ge1}\frac{a}{3^i}=\frac a2.
\]
As the left side is an integer,
\[
v_3(a!)\le\left\lfloor\frac a2\right\rfloor=n,
\tag{14}
\]
because \(a=2n+1\). Combining (13) and (14),
\[
\begin{aligned}
3+2v_3(M!)
&=3+2a+2v_3(a!)\\
&\le 3+2(2n+1)+2n\\
&=6n+5=M.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (12), hence (10). Since \(v_3(108)=3\), we obtain
\[
v_3\bigl(108K!L!(M!)^2\bigr)
\le v_3\bigl((3K)!(3L)!\bigr).
\tag{15}
\]

### 4. Completion of the divisibility argument

Let \(p\) be any prime.

* If \(p=2\), the required valuation inequality is (9).
* If \(p=3\), it is (15).
* If \(p\ne2,3\), then \(p\nmid108\), so \(v_p(108)=0\). The general factorial-ratio inequality (3), with \(M=K+L\), gives
  \[
  v_p\bigl(108K!L!(M!)^2\bigr)
  =v_p(K!)+v_p(L!)+2v_p(M!)
  \le v_p((3K)!)+v_p((3L)!).
  \]

Thus every prime occurs in \(108K!L!(M!)^2\) with exponent no larger than its exponent in \((3K)!(3L)!\). Therefore
\[
108K!L!(M!)^2\mid(3K)!(3L)!.
\]
Substituting back \(K=4n+2\), \(L=2n+3\), and \(M=6n+5\), we conclude that
\[
108(4n+2)!(2n+3)!((6n+5)!)^2
\mid
(12n+6)!(6n+9)!.
\]
Consequently
\[
\frac{(12n+6)!(6n+9)!}
{108(4n+2)!(2n+3)!((6n+5)!)^2}
\]
is an integer for every nonnegative integer \(n\), as required.
